articles.title: Pence: Stopping ballistic attacks in Ukraine will ‘take the last fighting tool out of Vladimir Putin’s hands’
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday stressed the importance of Ukraine having the capabilities to deter Russian ballistic missile strikes. During an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Pence said Russian forces have “shifted” to using high-arc ballistic missiles and cruise missiles to strike Ukraine. Those weapons require Patriot…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday stressed the importance of Ukraine having the capabilities to deter Russian ballistic missile strikes .

During an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Pence said Russian forces have “shifted” to using high-arc ballistic missiles and cruise missiles to strike Ukraine.

Those weapons require Patriot interceptors or terminal high-altitude area defense (THAAD) interceptors, the former vice president noted. Pence on Sunday addressed the National Prayer Breakfast in Ukraine and spoke with Zelensky.

“And President Zelensky again reiterated to me what he said publicly, that he’s anxious to see the United States make up to 5 percent of our Patriot resources available to make it possible for Ukraine to beat back those ballistic missile attacks,” Pence told host Chris Stirewalt.

“Stopping those ballistic missile attacks essentially will in many ways take the last fighting tool out of Vladimir Putin’s hands,” he said, referring to the Russian president.

While President Trump granted Ukraine a license to co-produce Patriot missiles in July, analysts have emphasized it will take years before the eastern European country is able to produce a suitable amount of those weapons.

Also complicating matters is the fact that the U.S. has exhausted nearly 80 percent of its THAAD interceptors and roughly half of its Patriots during the Iran war, CNN reported earlier this month .

Pence, though, denied Sunday that the Pentagon depleting its interceptor stockpiles is hurting Ukraine.

“I don’t see it that way, and I don’t think … the Ukrainians do either,” Pence told host Dana Bash on CNN’s “ State of the Union .”

July marked the deadliest month for civilians in Ukraine since May 2022, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.

Zelensky said Sunday he briefed Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and James Lankford (R-Okla.) in Kyiv on Russia’s “ongoing ballistic missile terror.”

The Ukrainian leader wrote on social media : “It is very important for Ukraine to have the capabilities to counter this, and implementing the decision to grant licenses for the production of Patriots could significantly help.”

Pence echoed Zelensky’s rhetoric, saying it is “essential” for the Trump administration and other foreign allies to continue backing Ukraine militarily.

Without further assistance, an “unprotected” Ukraine will be at risk of Russian attacks on energy infrastructure sites as the winter approaches, the former vice president stated.

“President Zelensky made it clear to me that Putin is going to use those ballistic missiles to strike, particularly not just like he did at a children’s hospital this week and not just as he did it at … a shopping mall this week,” Pence told Stirewalt. “But he’ll use that to take out the energy infrastructure here as winter approaches.”

articles.title: Donalds says he’s ‘working’ with Haitian leaders to stabilize government after end of TPS
articles.summary: Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), the GOP nominee for Florida governor, said Sunday he is “working” with leaders in Haiti to stabilize the country after the temporary protected status (TPS) of more than 300,000 Haitians migrants in the U.S. expired. “I’ve actually had meetings with the transitional government and the ambassador for the transitional government,” Donalds…
articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), the GOP nominee for Florida governor, said Sunday he is “working” with leaders in Haiti to stabilize the country after the temporary protected status (TPS) of more than 300,000 Haitians migrants in the U.S. expired.

“I’ve actually had meetings with the transitional government and the ambassador for the transitional government,” Donalds told host Margaret Brennan on CBS News’s “ Face the Nation .”

“They’re working on security forces right now as we speak to begin to stabilize Haiti, they’ve gotten about a quarter to half of the country under control from the gangs that basically took over Haiti,” added the Florida congressman, who won the Republican gubernatorial primary on Tuesday.

The Supreme Court earlier this summer allowed the Trump administration to revoke the TPS designation for Haitian migrants .

The high court ruled in a 6-3 decision, along ideological lines, that federal judges had no authority to weigh in on a challenge to the administration’s action brought by the migrants — reversing the February decision by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes to pause the revocation .

Roughly 158,000 Haitian TPS holders lived in Florida as of January, according to a report from the immigration advocacy group Fwd.us .

Haitian TPS holders contribute $2.6 billion annually to the Sunshine State’s economy, with 93,000 Haitians in Florida working in industries such as agriculture, security and nursing, the report noted.

The Obama administration initially granted Haitians TPS in 2010 after an earthquake struck the Caribbean island. The State Department still warns Americans against traveling to Haiti over risks associated with crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited healthcare.

But Donalds argued Sunday the TPS designation was not intended to last “into perpetuity with no end,” adding that creates the “wrong incentives to make sure that people can return to their home country, stabilize that country, and make sure that it returns to normalcy.”

articles.title: Sailor aboard USS Abraham Lincoln decries father’s ICE detention
articles.summary: A sailor on board the USS Abraham Lincoln on Saturday said his father was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Joshua Aviles has spent roughly nine months deployed at sea in support of the Iran war amid reported shortages of clean water, food and supplies. “I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at…
articles.body:
A sailor on board the USS Abraham Lincoln on Saturday said his father was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Joshua Aviles has spent roughly nine months deployed at sea in support of the Iran war amid reported shortages of clean water, food and supplies.

“I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything,” Aviles wrote in a post on Facebook.

“I just got a call that my dad was taken by ICE. If you know my dad, you know he is a hardworking, humble man who is always willing to help anyone if he can. My dad has his driver’s license, Social Security card, and work permit,” he added.

Aviles said his father was waiting to get his green card approved at the time he was detained. DHS confirmed his father, Luis Manuel Aviles Roa, was detained by immigration authorities on Saturday during a vehicle stop in Key West, Fla.

Authorities say they are unsure when he entered the U.S. but say he originated from Nicaragua.

“Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws. Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill.

“We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress. This Administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce,” a DHS spokesperson said, adding that “work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States.”

Aviles says having his father detained by immigration authorities is “heartbreaking.”

“This is heartbreaking for me. I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal,” Aviles wrote in the Facebook post.

“My dad’s only ‘crime’ was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life,” he added.

Aviles’s comments come after Democrats reported that under President Trump, ICE has arrested 125 veterans and attempted to deport at least 282 veterans and family members.

“Aside from legal concerns, DoD’s new practices create a chilling effect on service members and their families, who may avoid accessing bases, medical care, housing offices, or support services — or leave the military entirely — out of fear that routine interactions could lead to detention or deportation,” Democratic lawmakers wrote in their letter , which was obtained by The Hill and sent to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ on Iran puts China in the crosshairs
articles.summary: President Trump’s announcement of a major economic warfare campaign against Iran also has the effect of putting China in the crosshairs, the Islamic republic’s largest trading partner and primary purchaser of its oil exports. Trump’s threats to go after any country, business or banking institution supporting Iran come as diplomatic efforts have unraveled, six months…
articles.body:
President Trump’s announcement of a major economic warfare campaign against Iran also has the effect of putting China in the crosshairs, the Islamic republic’s largest trading partner and primary purchaser of its oil exports.

Trump’s threats to go after any country, business or banking institution supporting Iran come as diplomatic efforts have unraveled, six months of military pressure have failed to cow the Islamic republic and transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains a dangerous gamble.

While Trump held back from calling out China specifically in a Truth Social post on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was blunt, calling for the Chinese “to get with the program.”

“We are confident that everyone wants the strait reopened and for energy prices to come back down … keep in mind that the Chinese get 50 percent — 5-0 — of their energy from inside, from the gulf. So it would do them a big service to get with the program,” he said Thursday in an interview with CNBC.

Bessent said he will hold a press conference Monday to detail the administration’s game plan.

“Sanctions and pressure tactics are not the solution. China calls on parties to act responsibly and stick to the political and diplomatic approach,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said when asked by Bloomberg about the impact on China.

Analysts are cautious on whether Trump’s threats of economic “D-Day” against Iran and its enablers will bear fruit — and whether the president is determined to follow through with punishing economic actions against China ahead of a state visit for President Xi Jinping on Sept. 24.

Trump is eager for China to follow through on buying American agriculture, Boeing jets and U.S. oil, as well as preserve American access to Beijing’s supply of critical minerals — essential components of U.S. weapons production that have been depleted by the war.

“A much larger move against China one month before a leader-level summit in Washington would carry real diplomatic risk, invite a Chinese counterresponse and potentially put the meeting itself under pressure,” said Craig Singleton, senior fellow at the nonpartisan Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

Trump imposed earlier sanctions against so-called Chinese teapot refineries — small-to-medium independent plants processing Iranian oil — as part of the economic pressure campaign against Tehran. But Beijing rejected those sanctions and told blacklisted refineries to ignore the U.S. penalties.

“If the administration is unwilling to target the larger Chinese entities and financial channels sustaining Iranian trade, it is hard to see sanctions alone bringing Tehran to its knees,” Singleton continued.

He pointed to Russia as an example. While broad, international sanctions have imposed economic hardship, Moscow has demonstrated resilience by relying heavily on countries — like China — holding back sanctions to avoid economic collapse.

“‘Economic D-Day’ sounds dramatic, but it may say more about shrinking options than expanding leverage,” Singleton said.

“The military campaign has produced diminishing returns, so Trump is pivoting from missiles to markets. The harder question is whether Washington is actually willing to impose costs on major Chinese actors and risk disrupting the trade truce before the summit.”

Likewise, Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran, said the administration’s sanctions are a very strong warning to China and its banks enabling Iran, but “the proof will be in the follow-through and enforcement.”

And Josh Lipsky, vice president and chair in international economics at the Atlantic Council, told Bloomberg News that Trump’s threats against Iran are likely to fall flat absent close coordination with Europe and Chinese banks willing to cut off Tehran. He also raised both Trump’s and Xi’s desires for a good visit in September.

“It’s unclear to me how we’re going to choke off Iran more than we have financially without triggering immense blowback from China on the eve of President Xi’s visit to Washington, which has been so carefully choreographed over many months now,” he said.

The last face-to-face between Trump and Xi occurred in May in Beijing. The summit was regarded as successful in maintaining relationship stability and avoiding major ruptures. The leaders discussed the U.S. war against Iran, and Trump told reporters at the time that Xi said he feels strongly that Iran can’t have a nuclear weapon — one of the administration’s stated priorities for starting the war on Feb. 28 — “and he wants them to open up the strait.”

The U.S. has blacklisted 366 entities based in China and Hong Kong for evading sanctions on Iran, the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission wrote in a March fact sheet.

The fact sheet also noted a network of front companies and small regional banks in China and Hong Kong helps Iran launder most of the renminbi — Chinese currency — proceeds from the oil sales into the global financial system.

But while China helped push Iran to a ceasefire with the U.S. in April, there are few signals that Beijing wants to intervene again.

“When a conflict involves major military powers and China is not the cause of the war or a party to it, Beijing generally sees neither a particular responsibility nor a realistic possibility of becoming the primary mediator,” Zhao wrote.

articles.title: Bessent doubles down on Trump warnings: ‘Entering the endgame’ on Iran
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday previewed the Trump administration’s economic offensive against Iran, set to begin Monday. Echoing President Trump’s rhetoric on the military operations against the Islamic Republic, Bessent said the U.S. has “dismantled Iran’s capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program.” The Treasury secretary wrote…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday previewed the Trump administration’s economic offensive against Iran, set to begin Monday.

Echoing President Trump’s rhetoric on the military operations against the Islamic Republic , Bessent said the U.S. has “dismantled Iran’s capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program.”

The Treasury secretary wrote on social media , “We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”

Bessent is expected to address the looming sanctions in a press conference Monday afternoon.

Trump said last week his administration will undertake a “CRUSHING” economic operation against Iran, equating it to “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

In a post on Truth Social , the president warned other countries that allowing their “financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran” would result in economic consequences.

In conjunction with the military strikes against Iran, the Treasury Department has targeted the regime financially via its “ Operation Economic Fury ” initiative.

Among other actions, the department has frozen Iranian assets around the world, cracked down on the regime’s shadow banking networks and sanctioned the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, which the Iranian government created to handle shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

On Sunday, Bessent said the latest economic operation will “leverage every agency, every authority and action many assumed we would never summon.”

He added, “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

In advance of the economic operation from Washington, Iran’s rial currency dipped to a record-low 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar early Monday morning, The Associated Press reported.

articles.title: 76 percent in Canada say ending US trade negotiations was right call: Survey
articles.summary: More than three-quarters of Canadians believe their country ending trade negotiations with the U.S. was the right call, according to a new poll. In the Angus Reid Institute poll, 76 percent of respondents said their country was in the right “by refusing the terms being offered and ending negotiations without a trade agreement,” while 13…
articles.body:
More than three-quarters of Canadians believe their country ending trade negotiations with the U.S. was the right call, according to a new poll .

In the Angus Reid Institute poll , 76 percent of respondents said their country was in the right “by refusing the terms being offered and ending negotiations without a trade agreement,” while 13 percent said the opposite. Eleven percent were unsure about Canada’s decision.

On Friday evening, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney removed his country’s negotiators from trade discussions with the U.S., shortly before a new round of tariffs from the Trump administration went into effect.

The Canadian prime minister then said Saturday his country would implement retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. starting Sept. 8, responding to the Trump administration’s new 50 percent duties. The American tariffs impose a 50 percent levy on more than $20 billion’s worth of goods from the U.S.’s northern neighbor, impacting products like wine and cement.

During a press conference, Carney said Ottawa would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

President Trump on Sunday claimed Canada desires the “benefits of being a state, without being one” in a Truth Social post, referencing his previous talk of acquiring the country as the U.S.’s 51st state.

In the Angus Reid Institute poll, 6 percent said they were “very confident” in the idea “that Canada and the United States will eventually be able to reach a new trade agreement,” while 33 percent were “confident,” 48 percent were “not confident” and 14 percent were unsure about their confidence level.

The Angus Reid Institute poll took place from Aug. 22-23, featuring 1,468 Canadian adults and a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

articles.title: Democrats demand Iran war cost details from Trump, Hegseth
articles.summary: Nearly 50 House Democrats reportedly signed a letter to President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for more details on the cost of the Iran war. “What was billed as a two-week operation is now a full-scale war that has lasted for over 150 days, cost over $37 billion, and claimed the lives of…
articles.body:
Nearly 50 House Democrats reportedly signed a letter to President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for more details on the cost of the Iran war .

“What was billed as a two-week operation is now a full-scale war that has lasted for over 150 days, cost over $37 billion, and claimed the lives of 18 servicemembers,” the House Democrats wrote in the letter . “At the same time, prices across the country have gone up significantly, placing the burden of this conflict on American families.”

Democratic Reps. Jason Crow (Colo.), Maggie Goodlander (N.H.) and Derek Tran (Calif.) led the charge on the letter, per NBC. The trio served in the military and co-chair House Democrats’ national security task force.

“The Iranian regime — which for 47 years has chanted ‘Death to America’ and threatened our troops overseas — can never be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon, and the President’s team will continue to communicate with Congress as we work toward this shared goal,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told The Hill.

Trump initially said the Iran war would take roughly a month, but the conflict has stretched on for nearly six months without a lasting peace deal between his administration and Iranian leaders. The administration on Monday is ramping up its economic offensive against Iran.

In late July, Hegseth told the Senate Appropriations Committee the conflict had cost roughly $37.5 billion. When reached for comment on the letter from House Democrats, a Pentagon official referred The Hill to that price tag.

But NBC News reported earlier that month the Pentagon’s internal cost estimate of the war was $80 billion to $100 billion when accounting for the costs of repairing damaged military bases, replacing destroyed aircraft and fully replenishing weapons stockpiles.

White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought also asked Congress for $67.1 billion in June for the Pentagon. That included $1.7 billion for readiness, $17.3 billion for operational costs and $21 billion for munitions. The military has depleted its weapons stockpiles during the Middle Eastern conflict.

The war has come with financial costs for Americans, particularly due to the Iranian military’s restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.09 as of Monday , up from less than $3 two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the conflict, according to AAA.

“It is unconscionable that the Administration is asking for more to fund the very thing that is raising costs for Americans,” the letter from the four dozen lawmakers added, referencing the White House’s supplemental funding request. “The Administration should be focused on ending the conflict and addressing the very real financial concerns of the American public.”

Trump said earlier this month it is worth it for Americans “to pay a tiny, little bit more” for gas so the U.S. military could ensure Iran cannot develop a nuclear weapon.

“So remember that, when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK. … I’ll never apologize, I did the right thing,” the president said at an event in Garden City, N.Y.

The Democratic lawmakers asked Trump and Hegseth for a “public, comprehensive assessment” of the economic impact of the war by Sept. 11.

That assessment, the representatives noted, should include all Pentagon operational costs, the impact on oil and energy markets and the macroeconomic effects imposed by the war, such as its impact on gross domestic product growth (GDP), inflation and supply chains.

Annual inflation has risen from 2.4 percent in February to 3.4 percent in July , as measured by the consumer price index .

U.S. GDP also increased at an annual rate of 1.5 percent in the second quarter after 2.1 percent growth in the first quarter, based on data released by the Bureau of Economic Analysis .

articles.title: Your Business Looks Strong on Paper. Cash Flow May Tell a Different Story. Here’s Why That Gap Matters More Than Ever.
articles.summary: Not all profits are created equal. Learn why free cash flow provides a clearer picture of business performance than adjusted EBITDA.
articles.body:
Entrepreneur Media LLC and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some products and services through the links below.

EBITDA remains an important measure of operating performance, but it's no longer enough now that financing is more expensive and capital is more selective.

Buyers and lenders stop asking, "How much EBITDA does the company generate?" and start asking, "How much cash actually reaches the bank account?"

Adjusted EBITDA may influence the opening valuation discussion. Free cash flow often determines how much confidence buyers have in the business — and how much they're ultimately willing to pay.

Not long ago, almost every conversation about business value began and ended with EBITDA .

Management presentations highlighted it. Investment bankers built valuation discussions around it. Buyers compared multiples against it. Owners proudly pointed to year-over-year improvements as evidence that the business had become more valuable.

EBITDA remains an important measure of operating performance. But if there's one lesson the private markets have reinforced over the past few years, it's this: EBITDA is no longer enough.

When financing becomes more expensive and capital more selective, the conversation changes. Buyers and lenders stop asking, "How much EBITDA does the company generate?" and start asking, "How much cash actually reaches the bank account?"

That is where free cash flow separates itself from adjusted earnings.

EBITDA starts the conversation. Cash finishes it.

EBITDA was never designed to represent cash. It removes interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to provide a clearer view of operating performance before financing and accounting choices influence the result.

As a benchmarking tool, it's incredibly useful. The challenge begins when EBITDA is treated as though it were cash. It isn't.

A company can report impressive EBITDA while simultaneously consuming cash through rising working capital , heavy maintenance capital expenditures or inefficient operations. On paper, the business appears stronger than its bank account suggests.

No lender gets repaid with EBITDA. Debt is serviced with cash.

Why EBITDA often becomes a matter of judgment

During a transaction, EBITDA rarely remains the simple number reported in the financial statements.

It evolves into Adjusted EBITDA , where management identifies expenses they believe are non-recurring or not reflective of ongoing operations. These might include one-time legal costs, restructuring expenses, unusual owner compensation or acquisition-related costs.

articles.title: Canada’s opposition leader demands Carney reconvene Parliament after US trade talks collapse
articles.summary: Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre pressed his country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, to reconvene the Canadian Parliament amid trade tensions with the U.S. “As Canadians are vulnerable to an escalating trade war with the United States, Parliament must be reconvened. Canadians deserve answers on how trade talks collapsed, what tariffs will cost their families, and…
articles.body:
Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre pressed his country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, to reconvene the Canadian Parliament amid trade tensions with the U.S.

“As Canadians are vulnerable to an escalating trade war with the United States, Parliament must be reconvened. Canadians deserve answers on how trade talks collapsed, what tariffs will cost their families, and how their jobs will be protected,” Poilievre, the leader of Canada’s Conservative Party in the Canadian Parliament, said Monday in a post on the social platform X .

“Prime Minister, reconvene Parliament now,” he added.

Poilievre’s post also featured a letter to Carney in which the opposition leader said that “the failure to secure a durable trade agreement, together with escalating tariffs, now threatens deeper economic pain on top of a decade of rising costs and zero economic growth in the Canadian economy.”

Carney removed Canadian negotiators from trade discussions with the U.S. on Friday, shortly before a fresh round of tariffs from the Trump administration went into effect. He said a day later that his country would implement retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. starting on Sept. 8, responding to the new 50 percent tariffs from the Trump administration.

During a press conference, Carney said Canada would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Throughout President Trump’s second term, tensions have erupted between the U.S. and Canada, two countries that have historically shared a strong alliance, over tariff policy. The president has also pushed for Canada to become the U.S.’s 51st state, to Canadian opposition.

The Hill has reached out to Carney’s office for comment.

articles.title: Bessent warns Iran’s global partners to cut ties or face ‘Operation Economic Outcast’
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday issued a global warning for countries to cut any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system, launching a new economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic as the military front has reached a stalemate six months into the war. Called “Operation Economic…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday issued a global warning for countries to cut any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system, launching a new economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic as the military front has reached a stalemate six months into the war.

Called “Operation Economic Outcast,” the campaign is marketed as a financial “D-Day” akin to the American invasion of Normandy in World War II. But Bessent’s highly anticipated remarks offered few specific, public actions and instead appeared to serve as a stern advisory.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded to a question on the lack of specifics or immediate action.

He said President Trump is making calls to world leaders and that officials from the Defense, Treasury and State departments are calling counterparts demanding action in severing ties with Tehran.

Bessent held back naming and shaming specific governments or publicizing timelines for action but said they are being communicated behind the scenes.

“We’re not going to name names. We’ve already seen some results, and I am confident the president, as you all know, is quite persuasive,” Bessent said at a press conference announcing the sanctions plan.

“I would expect that very quickly, if they do not respond, then you will see the ramifications of their actions.”

Absent from Bessent’s remarks was whether the administration will take specific action against China, Iran’s largest trading partner and primary destination for its oil exports — although these have declined sharply over the course of the war. Trump is scheduled to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit on Sept. 24, where the two want to advance a trade deal.

Bessent said no country “is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” when asked if the administration was pulling punches on Beijing.

“We find that the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy, and we are level-setting with every country to tell them our expectations,” he said.

The administration has earlier sanctioned Chinese entities processing Iranian oil.

Alongside the announcement, the Treasury Department outlined that it was expanding its authority to sanction any person, regardless of location, for operating in specific sectors of the Iranian economy. These include digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. It further announced new sanctions against 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs, its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

“Treasury has mapped every node, every facilitator, and every network that Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions,” Bessent said.

He called for international branches of Iran’s Bank Melli closed and further teased that a major announcement of sanctions against a financial institution would take place by the end of the week.

The secretary projected the choice before Iran as “complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy.”

Trump has said his aim of going to war with Iran at the end of February was to prevent the country from ever building a nuclear weapon. But Iran has withstood six months of U.S. military attacks — initially in coordination with Israel — demonstrated its ability to hold the Strait of Hormuz hostage and walked away from diplomatic talks with the U.S. over its nuclear program.

The U.S. has responded by imposing a naval blockade against Iran in the strait, which has severely diminished the amount of Iranian oil exported by sea.

Iran’s currency, the rial, reached a record low Monday, declining to approximately 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. Trump, in a post on his social media site Truth Social, said Iran is “in Economic and Military Death Spiral.” In a separate post he said “IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!”

But Iran’s ability to militarily threaten ships in the Strait of Hormuz has created an effective chokehold on the key maritime waterway, raising energy prices globally and stifling Persian Gulf energy exports. A U.S. campaign to escort ships out of the strait has failed to restore transit to prewar levels.

Gas prices in the U.S. again reached over $4 per gallon in the last month, according to AAA.

Iran’s Parliament speaker who earlier negotiated with the U.S., Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, pushed back on the U.S. economic pressure campaign in a statement posted to the social platform X.

“Americans know that no one buys their bombast; the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” he wrote .

“Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere.”

Still, while the United Arab Emirates attempted a rapprochement with Iran, Abu Dhabi announced last week it was cutting trade ties with Tehran after coming under renewed military attacks.

articles.title: Prince Harry quits African conservation charity after rangers’ human rights abuses
articles.summary: African Parks was embroiled in scandal after it admitted that some of its rangers committed human rights violations.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Prince Harry has resigned from another African charity , marking his second exit from an Africa-focused charity in over a year.

The Duke of Sussex has resigned from the board of wildlife charity African Parks ahead of his move back to the United Kingdom, his spokesperson told The Independent .

African Parks was embroiled in scandal last year after it admitted that some of its rangers committed human rights violations.

One allegation accused a guard of beating, raping and torturing Baka people living in Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Republic of Congo.

Harry’s representative told The Independent that he still supports African Parks.

“The Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said. “His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”

Harry served six years as president of the conservation organizations and joined its board of directors in 2023.

In May, Survival International, an indigenous rights charity, urged Harry to resign from the African Parks board after he attended a fundraiser for the organization in Scottsdale, Ariz., drawing criticism from the group.

“It is outrageous to see Harry’s continued support to African Parks despite the horrific human rights abuses committed by its rangers against the Baka,” Survival International Director Caroline Pearce told the British newspaper The Times .

In March 2025, Harry stepped down from Sentebale, the charity he co-founded in Lesotho, Africa, in what he called a breakdown in leadership.

The charity’s chair, Dr. Sophie Chandauka, accused the charity of fostering an environment rife with abuse, including accusing Harry of coordinating a campaign of bullying and harassment.

Sentebale sued Harry, as well as another trustee, for defamation.

articles.title: Iran warns vessels of fines, detention for violating Strait of Hormuz rules
articles.summary: Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) on Sunday warned that it will fine and detain commercial vessels accused of violating its protocols for passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The PGSA stated on social media that 45 named vessels have been blacklisted and could have their cargoes confiscated. “Effective immediately, any vessel cooperating with listed…
articles.body:
Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) on Sunday warned that it will fine and detain commercial vessels accused of violating its protocols for passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

The PGSA stated on social media that 45 named vessels have been blacklisted and could have their cargoes confiscated.

“Effective immediately, any vessel cooperating with listed vessels … will be added to the list,” the PGSA wrote on the social platform X, adding that the owners of these vessels can submit a formal application to request their removal from the blacklist.

Some of the ships on the PGSA’s blacklist include several ships owned by the United Arab Emirates’s ADNOC Logistics and Services and Saudi Arabia’s national shipping carrier Bahri, Reuters reported .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned countries on Monday to cut their financial ties with Iran as the U.S. carries out “Operation Economic Outcast,” marketed as an “economic D-Day,” in reference to the U.S. invasion of Normandy Beach in World War II.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded to a question about the lack of details about the plan.

Bessent said that President Trump was making calls to world leaders, with the Defense, Treasury and State departments contacting their counterparts with the same warning.

Trump hinted at the “economic D-Day” last week, saying it would be a “CRUSHING” economic operation against Iran.

The PGSA was also targeted, with the Treasury Department sanctioning the new body out of Tehran, one of 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs and its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

The Trump administration said its goal in going to war with Iran since Feb. 28 was to prevent it from developing and obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has retaliated militarily over the last six months while also shutting down the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly 30 percent of the world’s crude oil is exported.

Iran’s hold over the strait has caused global gas prices and inflation to rise. The national average for gas in the U.S. reached $4.09 per gallon on Monday, nearly $1 more than the average last year, according to data from AAA .

Negotiations to reopen the strait and permanently end the war have stalled after both countries initially signed an interim peace deal in June. After a period last month when both countries exchanged strikes, Trump has vowed to crush Iran through economic warfare.

Bessent hinted Sunday that this economic warfare will usher in a final phase of the conflict.

“We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: Putin wants to mobilize at least 300,000 more troops to Russia-Ukraine war: Zelensky
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that Russian President Vladimir Putin plans to draft 300,000 more troops in his continued war effort against Ukraine. Zelensky told reporters Russia could draft enough troops next year to reach a total of 500,000, according to Reuters. Russian forces have recently ramped up ballistic missile strikes against Ukraine, targeting…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that Russian President Vladimir Putin plans to draft 300,000 more troops in his continued war effort against Ukraine.

Zelensky told reporters Russia could draft enough troops next year to reach a total of 500,000, according to Reuters .

Russian forces have recently ramped up ballistic missile strikes against Ukraine, targeting several cities, including Kyiv. July marked the deadliest month for civilians in Ukraine since May 2022, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.

“We see what Putin is doing and what he wants,” Zelensky said Monday on Ukrainian Independence Day, marking 35 years since Ukraine seceded from the Soviet Union.

“A solution to his ballistic terror must be found, and this gamble of his must not pay off,” the Ukrainian leader added, referring to Putin.

To combat the Russian ballistic missile threats, Zelensky has urged the Trump administration to set aside 5 percent of its remaining Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine.

While President Trump granted Ukraine a license to co-produce Patriots in July, analysts have emphasized it will take years before the European nation can produce enough of those weapons to adequately combat Russian ballistics.

The Pentagon has exhausted roughly half of its Patriot missiles during the Iran war, CNN reported earlier this month.

Zelensky has also discussed surging foreign military assistance with other foreign leaders, including during a Monday meeting with European officials, a group Zelensky dubbed the “coalition of the willing.”

“Russia continues its attacks and ballistic missiles — yesterday, we spoke about it, with details. Today we will continue,” Zelensky remarked during the gathering . “So we need to make sure that the winter package of air defense will be in Ukraine.”

“And we need the winter package of Patriot missiles. We hope that we will have this package — we need at least 300 Patriot missiles for the winter and for the cold months.”

As of late July, the U.S. military had between 759 and 827 Patriots, down from 2,330 the day before the Iran conflict began, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies .

Over the last month, the Pentagon has awarded contracts to Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin to boost production of Patriot interceptor parts.

articles.title: US formally removes Syria’s designation as State Sponsor of Terrorism
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Monday formally removed Syria from its state sponsor of terrorism (SST) list, an extraordinary milestone for the government of Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former terrorist turned statesman who led the campaign to overthrow the dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad. The removal of the SST designation provides enormous sanctions relief for Syria and the…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Monday formally removed Syria from its state sponsor of terrorism (SST) list, an extraordinary milestone for the government of Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former terrorist turned statesman who led the campaign to overthrow the dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad.

The removal of the SST designation provides enormous sanctions relief for Syria and the ability for Damascus to fully rejoin the international financial system. The country faces huge challenges in reconstruction following more than a decade of civil war. The U.S. is also delisting al-Sharaa’s group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), from the specially designated global terrorist (SDGT) list.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the removal of the SST label recognized “positive actions and further commitments” by the Syrian government under al-Sharaa to fully distance the country from acts of international terrorism. Syria was initially put on the list in 1979. Only three other countries are SST — Cuba, Iran and North Korea.

“Rescinding Syria’s designation as an SST and HTS’ designation as an SDGT eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy,” Rubio said in a statement.

The World Bank estimated Syria’s reconstruction costs at $216 billion in a report published in October 2025.

On Monday, Trump posted on Truth Social a photo of al-Sharaa and Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani holding the president’s signed executive order that directed sanctions relief on Syria.

Tom Barrack, U.S. ambassador to Turkey and Syria special envoy, described removing the SST designation as ushering in a new era of U.S.-Syrian relations.

“For too long, this designation was another wall separating the Syrian people from the investment, enterprise, and opportunity necessary to rebuild their nation. Today, another wall comes down,” he wrote on social media .

“Capital can replace conflict, enterprise can replace isolation, and commerce can continue to triumph over chaos.”

There is overwhelming bipartisan support for the Trump administration’s sanctions relief on Syria, despite reservations over whether al-Sharaa had shed his terrorist past. Since taking over the country in December 2024, al-Sharaa has renounced his former ties with al Qaeda and the Islamic State and has used close relationships with Turkey and Saudi Arabia to appeal to Trump.

But some lawmakers have raised concern about instances of sectarian violence, Syrian ties with Russia and fair representation in Syria’s new government.

articles.title: Raskin: ‘Trump’s idiotic trade war killing American businesses’
articles.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) on Sunday went after President Trump for his recent tariffs on Canada. “Stop Trump’s idiotic trade war killing American businesses. Let peaceful commerce among the nations prevail. And hands off Canada, America’s #1 trading partner, whose people are now boycotting American products because of Trump’s imbecilic policies,” Raskin said in a…
articles.body:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) on Sunday went after President Trump for his recent tariffs on Canada.

“Stop Trump’s idiotic trade war killing American businesses. Let peaceful commerce among the nations prevail. And hands off Canada, America’s #1 trading partner, whose people are now boycotting American products because of Trump’s imbecilic policies,” Raskin said in a post on the social platform X.

Raskin’s comments come in the wake of heated trade-related tensions between Washington and Ottawa.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday removed Canadian negotiators from trade discussions with the U.S., shortly before the Trump administration’s new set of tariffs went into effect.

A day later, Carney said his country would implement retaliatory tariffs against the U.S.’s new 50 percent tariffs starting Sept. 8.

During a press conference, Carney said Canada would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Raskin isn’t the only Democratic critic of the recent U.S. trade tensions with Canada, with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) saying Sunday that Trump is “destroying the relationship with one of our country’s strongest allies.”

“Since Day One, Donald Trump has chosen chaos and cruelty — and by doubling down on his reckless trade war with Canada, he’s further harming our families, farmers, and small business owners,” Shapiro said in a post on X.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Ontario’s Ford warns US power could be cut as he trades insults with Trump
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Monday threatened to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S. as a trade war with President Trump plays out publicly for a second time. Ford told reporters “everything is on the table” when it comes to retaliatory measures against the White House in response to failed trade talks and…
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Monday threatened to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S. as a trade war with President Trump plays out publicly for a second time.

Ford told reporters “everything is on the table” when it comes to retaliatory measures against the White House in response to failed trade talks and heightened tariffs .

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses. Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes,” Ford said at a Monday press conference.

“You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario,” he added.

Ontario’s power grid connects directly across the border to Michigan, New York and Minnesota. Ford has previously threatened to cut power to U.S. states during the fallout of trade negotiations last year.

Ultimately, at that time, he met with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and cooled tensions via bilateral talks.

However, pressures have resumed after Trump introduced a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.

Ottawa had already said it would respond with retaliatory tariffs before Ford launched his energy threat and proposed pulling U.S. access to Canada’s critical minerals.

Trump responded to the potential actions on Truth Social and called Ford the “overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” Doug’s older brother who served on city council and as mayor of Toronto.

The president said Canada was facing “bad leadership” primarily from Prime Minister Mark Carney and “Flunky Ford.”

He urged the two to “fall in line,” to which Ford said , “kiss my a‑‑.”

Canadian opposition leader Pierre Poilievre is urging politicians to tread lightly with the Trump administration.

“As Canadians are vulnerable to an escalating trade war with the United States, Parliament must be reconvened. Canadians deserve answers on how trade talks collapsed, what tariffs will cost their families, and how their jobs will be protected,” Poilievre, the leader of Canada’s Conservative Party in the Canadian Parliament, said Monday in a post on the social platform X .

articles.title: Zelensky says wartime election would ‘destroy’ Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that holding elections amid Russia’s war with Ukraine would “destroy” the country. “I believe that ​if we want to destroy the country, then we can move towards elections ​during this kind of war,” Zelensky told reporters. The president said elections “in general pose major risks,” noting that holding an…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that holding elections amid Russia’s war with Ukraine would “destroy” the country.

“I believe that ​if we want to destroy the country, then we can move towards elections ​during this kind of war,” Zelensky told reporters.

The president said elections “in general pose major risks,” noting that holding an election “right now would be a tsunami for the state, one that would divide Ukraine,” Politico reported .

“That’s why my strategy is to steer the country toward an ending of the war and to preserve an ⁠independent ​and sovereign state,” he added.

Ukrainian law bars the country from holding elections during wartime.

Polling released by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology earlier this month found that 57 percent of Ukrainians want to hold elections after the war ends.

Zelensky’s remarks come after ousted former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for a wartime poll in an address last week, NBC News reported. Zelensky said he thought some of Fedorov’s actions were misguided.

“I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” the president said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”

He appeared to link Fedorov to a meeting involving Starlink and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, where Fedorov told Zelensky that SpaceX agreed to have Ukraine use Starlink on Russian territory. Zelensky raised this with President Trump and later told him that Musk rejected the proposal, accusing him of having misled Trump.

Zelensky said that this incident was among the reasons behind “some of the steps” that led to Fedorov no longer being in his position.

Fedorov has emerged as a rival to Zelensky, telling Ukrainians Tuesday that the “people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made,” Politico reported.

The former minister doubled down on his address during a Sunday interview with the BBC . He told the outlet that Zelensky has “questions to answer” about corruption within the government. Fedorov also talked about Ukrainian elections, noting that “democracy should not be the hostage of” Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?” he told the broadcaster.

Zelensky was first elected in 2019, when he defeated incumbent President Petro Poroshenko in a landslide victory. He was a comedian and television personality before entering politics.

He said last December that Ukraine was ready for elections after Trump had said the same thing.

“Since this question is raised today by the president of the United States of America, our partners, I will answer very briefly,” Zelensky told U.S. reporters at the time after a phone call with Trump. “Look, I am ready for elections. … I personally have the will and readiness to do this.”

articles.title: Tarcísio diz que cumprirá decisão do STF para compartilhar documentos de ONG de 'Dark Horse' e nega atraso em investigação sobre o filme em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: O governador afirmou que a Polícia Civil cumprirá a ordem de Flávio Dino para compartilhar as provas com a PF e rebateu acusações de que as apurações sobre suspeitas de desvio de recursos para financiar o filme “Dark Horse” estejam sendo atrasadas.
articles.summary: O governador afirmou que a Polícia Civil cumprirá a ordem de Flávio Dino para compartilhar as provas com a PF e rebateu acusações de que as apurações sobre suspeitas de desvio de recursos para financiar o filme “Dark Horse” estejam sendo atrasadas.
articles.body:
O governador de São Paulo , Tarcísio de Freitas ( Republicanos ), disse nesta terça-feira (25) que a Polícia Civil vai cumprir a decisão judicial do STF e enviar à Polícia Federal os documentos apreendidos na operação de junho contra a ONG da dona da produtora do filme "Dark Horse".

O compartilhamento das provas é uma determinação do ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Flávio Dino, que deu o prazo de cinco dias para que as provas colhidas pela Polícia Civil Paulista na chamada Operação Wi-Fi sejam compartilhados com a PF, que investiga as empresas de Karina da Gama, dona da produtora Go Up que produziu o filme sobre o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

🔍 A operação foi realizada em junho deste ano e entre os alvos estava o Instituto Conhecer Brasil (ICB), que pertence a Karina Gama, dona do instituto e sócia da produtora Go UP , produtora do filme Dark Horse, uma cinebiografia sobre a trajetória do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

A Polícia Civil apura suspeitas de fraude em um contrato com a Prefeitura de São Paulo no valor de R$ 108 milhões por ano.

Os adversários de Tarcísio afirmam que, desde que a operção da Polícia Civil, os investigadores da polícia de SP têm atrasado as diligências por conta do período eleitoral, umas vez que as denúncias contra Karina da Gama, seu Instituto e sua produtora de cinema recebem verbas públicas de aliados do governador.

"Obviamente se tem uma decisão judicial, a decisão vai ser cumprida. As investigações seguem um ritmo estabelecido na lei. Temos profissionais a frente das investigações. A medida que as decisões judiciais forem aparecendo, elas vão sendo cumpridas", disse o governador de SP.

Tarcísio chamou de "desrespeito com a polícia" quem acusa os investigadores de "sentarem nas investigações" ou atrasarem as apurações contra a empresa produtora da filme, a Go UP Entertainment, de Karina da Gama, mesma dona do Instituto Conhecer Brasil (ICB), dona do contrato de instalação de pontos de wi-fi na cidade de São Paulo.

"A Polícia Civil é uma instituição profissional e é uma polícia de estado, não de governo. E a gente tem que ter confiança nas instituições de estado. Uma declaração ou acusação dessas mostra que há desapreço e desrespeito com as instituições policiais", afirmou Tarcísio.

Tarcísio em evento nesta terça-feira (25) — Foto: Divulgação

O secretário da Segurança Pública, Osvaldo Nico, que também estava no evento, confirmou que a Polícia Civil paulista deve remeter os documentos para a PF em Brasília ainda nesta terça-feira (25).

O g1 apurou que além de notas fiscais e contratos, a Polícia Civil paulista apreendeu em junho o celular de Karina da Gama, o computador pessoal dela e também pediu a quebra de sigilo fiscal da empresária e das empresas e institutos controlados por ela.

Candidato à reeleição em São Paulo pelo Republicanos, Tarcísio participou de um seminário da Guarda Civil Metropolitana (GCM) da capital paulista sobre combate à violência contra mulheres.

Ao lado do prefeito Ricardo Nunes (MDB), Tarcísio prometeu criar um cadastro estadual de agressores de mulheres, caso seja reeleito, além de triplicar o número de delegacias das mulheres que funcionam 24 horas no estado.

Atualmente, apenas 18 das 114 Delegacias de Defesa da Mulher funcionam ininterruptamente em São Paulo. A promessa dele é que esse número passe a 60 ao final dos próximos quatro anos de governo.

O governador Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) ao lado da esposa e do prefeito Ricardo Nunes (MDB), durante seminário da GCM na Zona Norte de SP. — Foto: Divulgação

A Polícia Civil de São Paulo informou que recebeu no fim da tarde desta segunda-feira (24) a decisão do ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), para compartilhar com a Polícia Federal dados e documentos apreendidos durante a Operação Wi-Fi .

Já no inquérito aberto pelo STF, os dados da operação serão usados para apurar a suspeita de que emendas parlamentares podem ter abastecido a produção de Dark Horse.

Segundo a determinação de Dino, a Polícia Civil tem prazo de cinco dias para fornecer os dados brutos, extrações de celulares e documentos apreendidos durante a operação.

A TV Globo apurou que o delegado responsável pela investigação em São Paulo já entrou em contato com o delegado da Coordenação de Inquéritos nos Tribunais Superiores, em Brasília, para providenciar a remessa do material o mais rápido possível.

Karina Ferreira da Gama, dona da empresa Go UP Entertainment, responsável pelo filme ‘Dark Horse’ - sobre a vida do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL). — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Ao STF, a PF argumentou que o instituto está no centro da apuração sobre emendas e que os elementos recolhidos pela Polícia Civil em endereços da ONG , da empresária Karina Ferreira da Gama e de outras empresas podem ajudar a aprofundar e até acelerar a investigação.

A ideia é que os investigadores possam analisar dados de computadores, celulares, documentos contábeis, notas fiscais, comprovantes de pagamentos e registros financeiros, que seriam relevantes para o inquérito. Foram liberados dados brutos e também relatórios já produzidos sobre as mídias apreendidas.

O ministro Flávio Dino considerou que o pedido e a justificativa da PF eram pertinentes e estavam de acordo com o entendimento do STF para esse tipo de compartilhamento.

O inquérito foi aberto depois que Dino pediu uma apuração da Controladoria-Geral da União sobre emendas dos deputados Mário Frias, Marcos Pollon, Bia Kicis destinadas ao Instituto Conhecer Brasil (ICB) e à Academia Nacional de Cultura (ANC), entidades alegadamente vinculadas a um mesmo núcleo de gestão coordenado por Karina Ferreira da Gama.

A PF está detalhando todas as relações empresariais de Karina e suas empresas, além de analisar eventuais doações eleitorais relacionadas aos investigados.

Vorcaro bancou mais de 90% do orçamento de filme sobre Jair Bolsonaro, diz dona da produtora

MP investiga contrato de R$ 108 milhões de wi-fi público da Prefeitura de SP com ONG de produtora do filme sobre Bolsonaro

articles.title: Trump’s tariff war with Canada threatens GOP candidates in border battlegrounds
articles.summary: President Trump’s tariff war with Canada is putting vulnerable GOP candidates in border states in a precarious position about 10 weeks out from the midterms, with economic anxiety already running high. Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports took effect on Saturday after bilateral negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour. Trump…
articles.body:
President Trump’s tariff war with Canada is putting vulnerable GOP candidates in border states in a precarious position about 10 weeks out from the midterms, with economic anxiety already running high.

Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports took effect on Saturday after bilateral negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour. Trump threatened 50 percent tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel on Monday to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Some strategists say the impact on Americans, particularly in states with close economic ties to Canada, will only compound GOP challenges around affordability, with voters losing trust in Republicans to handle the economy.

“This escalation and the timing of it are problematic,” Jason Cabel Roe, a Michigan-based Republican strategist, told The Hill.

“It really undermines our messaging when we’re trying to address affordability and we’re already having to deal with the price of oil due to the war in Iran. But that affordability debate only gets more complicated when we’re in a trade war with our largest trading partner, who happens to share a border with us,” he said.

Roe said the trade war could also be “an opportunity for Republicans to separate themselves from the president’s policy.”

The only GOP candidate to attempt to create that distance so far has been Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is facing a tough reelection race against Democrat Troy Jackson. She has consistently spoken out against Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, joining three other Republicans who voted with Democrats last year to undo tariffs on Canada.

This time around, she called the escalating tariffs a “mistake” and urged officials to get back to the negotiating table.

“The on-again/off-again trade talks between the U.S. and Canada lead to higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine businesses. If the Administration proceeds with these tariffs, they will increase costs for Maine families, as most businesses will have no choice but to pass on the tariffs to their customers through higher prices,” she wrote on the social platform X over the weekend.

The trade war also stands to become an issue in Ohio, where Sen. Jon Husted (R) is facing a challenge from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), and in Michigan’s open Senate race between former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Abdul El-Sayed (D). Democrats are also seeking to zero in on the issue in Iowa and Alaska, where they see opportunities to further expand the Senate map.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated all four races as toss-ups.

Wayne Winegarden, senior fellow in business and economics at the Pacific Research Institute, said the tariffs would make production more costly for U.S. businesses along the border, which would adjust in ways that ultimately hurt consumers and families in those states.

Vice President Vance defended the tariffs while rallying Republicans in Maine on Monday — an event that Collins skipped. He argued the administration was seeking to protect Mainers.

“I think that we need to send a message loud and clear to the prime minister of Canada: Stop taking advantage of the people of Maine. Stop taking advantage of America. It’s over, we expect fairness in our trade policy,” Vance said.

But Democrats see political opportunity in the coming repercussions of the tariff tit for tat.

“Americans are paying more for everything because GOP Senate candidates have served as a rubber stamp for Trump’s chaotic tariffs at the expense of their states. Come November, voters will hold them accountable for making life more expensive,” said Tommy Garcia, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Adrian Hemond, a Michigan-based Democratic strategist, said Ohio and especially Michigan rely on trade with Canada more than other states.

“The president’s ego may have disastrous effects for Republicans politically, but there’s no question that the economic results for Michigan and Ohio will be disastrous,” Hemond said.

Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate candidate in New Hampshire, is using the trade war to lash out at his Trump-backed Republican opponent, former Sen. John Sununu (N.H.).

“Trump creates a mess he can’t clean up. Once again,” Pappas wrote on social media on Saturday. “John Sununu won’t speak out against it. Once again.”

“Working families are paying for this recklessness,” he added.

The Cook Political Report has classified New Hampshire’s race as “lean Democratic.”

One Republican operative told The Hill that “every candidate has to run the race that they see fit.”

“They have to break with the administration when they see fit, when it benefits the state, and their region,” they said.

Canada rejected the U.S.’s terms for a trade deal late Friday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying last-minute additions by the U.S. were “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

Carney said Canada would “match those tariffs dollar for dollar” starting Sept. 8 and that “additional measures” would be taken to support workers and business owners in Canada.

The collapsed deal came after weeks of intense negotiations between the U.S. and Canada.

Canada is the U.S.’s second-largest trading partner. The 50 percent tariffs that took effect this weekend impact everything from wine to hockey sticks to cement.

“Those costs are at some point going to get passed down to their consumers,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute. “I don’t think something like inflation will pick up from these tariffs, but I think there’s going to be cost increases in specific sectors.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford told The Associated Press on Monday that Canada is “all in,” and he warned Republican states would face the brunt of the country’s retaliation.

“The red states we’re going to hit hard,” Ford told reporters Monday.

White House spokesperson Kush Desai defended the tariffs, saying, “President Trump ascended to the White House on a clear promise to the forgotten men and women of America that they would be forgotten no longer.”

“Countless American workers, farmers, and businesses have borne the brunt of America’s lopsided trade relations, including with Canada which has demanded total access to the American market without reciprocity. President Trump will never stop fighting to put Americans and America First,” he said.
paragraphs: President Trump’s tariff war with Canada is putting vulnerable GOP candidates in border states in a precarious position about 10 weeks out from the midterms, with economic anxiety already running high.

Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports took effect on Saturday after bilateral negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour. Trump threatened 50 percent tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel on Monday to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Some strategists say the impact on Americans, particularly in states with close economic ties to Canada, will only compound GOP challenges around affordability, with voters losing trust in Republicans to handle the economy.
“This escalation and the timing of it are problematic,” Jason Cabel Roe, a Michigan-based Republican strategist, told The Hill.

“It really undermines our messaging when we’re trying to address affordability and we’re already having to deal with the price of oil due to the war in Iran. But that affordability debate only gets more complicated when we’re in a trade war with our largest trading partner, who happens to share a border with us,” he said.
Roe said the trade war could also be “an opportunity for Republicans to separate themselves from the president’s policy.”

The only GOP candidate to attempt to create that distance so far has been Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is facing a tough reelection race against Democrat Troy Jackson. She has consistently spoken out against Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, joining three other Republicans who voted with Democrats last year to undo tariffs on Canada.
This time around, she called the escalating tariffs a “mistake” and urged officials to get back to the negotiating table.

“The on-again/off-again trade talks between the U.S. and Canada lead to higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine businesses. If the Administration proceeds with these tariffs, they will increase costs for Maine families, as most businesses will have no choice but to pass on the tariffs to their customers through higher prices,” she wrote on the social platform X over the weekend.

The trade war also stands to become an issue in Ohio, where Sen. Jon Husted (R) is facing a challenge from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), and in Michigan’s open Senate race between former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Abdul El-Sayed (D). Democrats are also seeking to zero in on the issue in Iowa and Alaska, where they see opportunities to further expand the Senate map.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated all four races as toss-ups.

Wayne Winegarden, senior fellow in business and economics at the Pacific Research Institute, said the tariffs would make production more costly for U.S. businesses along the border, which would adjust in ways that ultimately hurt consumers and families in those states.
Vice President Vance defended the tariffs while rallying Republicans in Maine on Monday — an event that Collins skipped. He argued the administration was seeking to protect Mainers.

“I think that we need to send a message loud and clear to the prime minister of Canada: Stop taking advantage of the people of Maine. Stop taking advantage of America. It’s over, we expect fairness in our trade policy,” Vance said.
But Democrats see political opportunity in the coming repercussions of the tariff tit for tat.

“Americans are paying more for everything because GOP Senate candidates have served as a rubber stamp for Trump’s chaotic tariffs at the expense of their states. Come November, voters will hold them accountable for making life more expensive,” said Tommy Garcia, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
Adrian Hemond, a Michigan-based Democratic strategist, said Ohio and especially Michigan rely on trade with Canada more than other states.
“The president’s ego may have disastrous effects for Republicans politically, but there’s no question that the economic results for Michigan and Ohio will be disastrous,” Hemond said.
Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate candidate in New Hampshire, is using the trade war to lash out at his Trump-backed Republican opponent, former Sen. John Sununu (N.H.).
“Trump creates a mess he can’t clean up. Once again,” Pappas wrote on social media on Saturday. “John Sununu won’t speak out against it. Once again.”
“Working families are paying for this recklessness,” he added.
The Cook Political Report has classified New Hampshire’s race as “lean Democratic.”
One Republican operative told The Hill that “every candidate has to run the race that they see fit.”
“They have to break with the administration when they see fit, when it benefits the state, and their region,” they said.

Canada rejected the U.S.’s terms for a trade deal late Friday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying last-minute additions by the U.S. were “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
Carney said Canada would “match those tariffs dollar for dollar” starting Sept. 8 and that “additional measures” would be taken to support workers and business owners in Canada.
The collapsed deal came after weeks of intense negotiations between the U.S. and Canada.
Canada is the U.S.’s second-largest trading partner. The 50 percent tariffs that took effect this weekend impact everything from wine to hockey sticks to cement.

“Those costs are at some point going to get passed down to their consumers,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute. “I don’t think something like inflation will pick up from these tariffs, but I think there’s going to be cost increases in specific sectors.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford told The Associated Press on Monday that Canada is “all in,” and he warned Republican states would face the brunt of the country’s retaliation.
“The red states we’re going to hit hard,” Ford told reporters Monday.

White House spokesperson Kush Desai defended the tariffs, saying, “President Trump ascended to the White House on a clear promise to the forgotten men and women of America that they would be forgotten no longer.”

“Countless American workers, farmers, and businesses have borne the brunt of America’s lopsided trade relations, including with Canada which has demanded total access to the American market without reciprocity. President Trump will never stop fighting to put Americans and America First,” he said.

articles.title: Canada expected to announce retaliatory tariffs Tuesday
articles.summary: Canada is expected to unveil retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. on Tuesday, following President Trump’s new threats to escalate the trade war between the two countries. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced his country would match U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar” after the Trump administration’s 50 percent tariffs on more than $20 billion worth of…
articles.body:
Canada is expected to unveil retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. on Tuesday, following President Trump’s new threats to escalate the trade war between the two countries.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced his country would match U.S. tariffs “ dollar for dollar ” after the Trump administration’s 50 percent tariffs on more than $20 billion worth of Canadian goods went into effect on Saturday. These retaliatory import taxes would go into effect on Sept. 8.

However, the Canadian leader said Monday the country may need to use more targeted retaliation to safeguard its workers and businesses after Trump threatened new 50 percent tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel that would take effect on New Year’s Day.

The president accused Canada of “ripping off the United States of America for years” in a Truth Social post.

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”

Carney, who pulled his country’s negotiators at the last minute from trade talks with the U.S. last Friday, accused the Trump administration of treating Canada as “a subsidiary of the United States” during trade discussions.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford reiterated his previous threat to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S. in response to escalating tensions between the two countries on Monday. The province’s power grid directly connects to Michigan, New York and Minnesota.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses. Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes,” he said during a press conference.

Trump lashed out at Ford and Carney in response, accusing the prime minister and “Flunky Ford” of “bad leadership.”

The president, who has repeatedly suggested Canada could be added as a “51st state,” said in a Truth Social post Tuesday morning that his administration was “giving serious consideration” to renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

But, the president added, he does not expect to be “doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

articles.title: Trump eyes changing Lake Ontario name amid trade war with Canada
articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday his administration is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, amid the trade war between the U.S. and Canada. “The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday his administration is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, amid the trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social .

It would not be the first time the president has sought to rename a body of water bordering the U.S. and another country. Last year, Trump signed an executive ordering renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America .

Trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa devolved into an all-out trade war over the weekend after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney removed negotiators from trade talks with the U.S.

Carney’s move came before a new set of tariffs from the Trump administration on Canada were set to go into effect.

The prime minister then announced that Ottawa would enact retaliatory tariffs in response to the U.S.’s new 50 percent tariffs starting Sept. 8. The Canadian leader said during a press conference that his nation would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford also lashed out at Trump over the levies, threatening on Monday to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford told reporters Monday. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”

“You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario,” he added.
